lesson_title: Lemons, Rocks and Airbags: the Limiting Reagent Game
hook_text: Twenty lemons. Six cups of sugar. Guess which one shuts the lemonade stand — most people get it wrong.
clip_script: The stand's recipe is non-negotiable: four lemons plus one cup of sugar makes one jug of lemonade. Saturday's stock: twenty lemons and six cups of sugar. How many jugs? The lazy answer stares at the smaller number — six — and blames the sugar. The correct move is the ratio test: twenty lemons demand five cups of sugar. Do we hold five? Yes — six. Sugar survives; the LEMONS run out first. Five jugs, then the stand goes quiet with one cup of sugar still unopened. That is the limiting reagent: the ingredient that dies first and closes the stand. And the same arithmetic sits inside your steering wheel. A pellet of sodium azide, lighter than a cricket ball, runs its recipe in a crash: two units of azide pay out THREE of nitrogen gas — fifty cubic decimetres of pillow in thirty milliseconds. Engineers sized that pellet with lemonade-stand arithmetic. Small does not mean limiting. The ratio decides — always.
visual_style: Top-down lemonade stand with lemon and sugar counters draining at different speeds, lemons flatlining first; smash cut to a steering wheel cross-section where a tiny pellet balloons into a full translucent airbag.
mood: Cheeky quiz energy pivoting into real-stakes engineering.
pacing: Rapid-fire setup, pause on the wrong instinct, ratio-test reveal, airbag escalation and out.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never lose a mark to the smaller-number trap.
